512.title: What does go
512.hook: the Name and good deeds go along (Sukhmani 19)
512.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting the nineteenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib hear that only the Name, earned through practice, goes along at the end; many sum up Guru Nanak's way as remembering the Name, honest work and sharing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dasvandh, and your line: left behind. Did you give one thing away? Yesterday the nineteenth ashtpadi listed what we leave. Today it answers the obvious next question. Day five hundred twelve.

At the airport check-in desk there's a scale, and a number on a sign: fifty pounds. Anything over that costs you, or stays home. So people kneel on the floor of the terminal, unzipping suitcases, pulling out the extra shoes, the heavy book, the jar of pickle from an aunt. It's a strange little moment of truth. What actually matters enough to carry? Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi has its own scale, and its own short list. Yesterday it said what stays behind. Today: what does go.
screen: `THE SCALE AT CHECK-IN.` → `WHAT MATTERS ENOUGH TO CARRY?` → `WHAT DOES GO.`

segments.voice: Go back two days, to the salok that opens the nineteenth ashtpadi. Its first line said nothing goes along without devotion. Its second line, in paraphrase, already holds today's answer: earn the Name of the Lord, says Nanak; this is the wealth worth having. Come back to the verb Guru Arjan picks: kamaavanaa, to earn. It's the ordinary Punjabi word for earning a living, for a day's wages. So the Name isn't pictured as a lottery ticket. It's earned the way bread is earned, by showing up, again and again, over years. And it's the one kind of savings the scale at the end can't weigh out. Then there's the second thing that travels: what you've done. Sikhs hear this in the closing salok of Japji, the morning prayer: by their own deeds, some come near and some go far. Guru Nanak's teaching is often summed up in three short phrases: remember the Name, earn honestly, and share what you have. Notice that two of the three are about how you treat other people. Read that way, the soul doesn't carry a trophy shelf, or a bank balance. It carries a character: what it became through the remembering and the giving. Kindness done is not a thing you own; it's something you've turned into. That's why it fits in the bag. And there's a quiet comfort in that list. You can't take the house or the title. But the part of you that learned to be generous? Read with Japji's closing line, that's the part that comes along.
screen: `THE SALOK: NOTHING ELSE GOES ALONG.` · `KAMAAVANAA: EARN IT LIKE WAGES.` · `YOUR DEEDS BRING YOU NEAR OR FAR.` · `YOU CARRY WHAT YOU BECAME.` · then, large: `KINDNESS TRAVELS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one lasting kindness. Not a quick like on a post, but something that will still be true next month. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one person who could use something real from you: an hour, a skill, a long-overdue apology, a recommendation letter, a regular phone call. Picture yourself doing it, all the way through. Then pick the first small step, and a time today to take it. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Karmee, by deeds: in Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi only the earned Name goes along, and in Sikh teaching karmee, our deeds, bring us near or far.
Your line: kindness travels. Today, take the first step of that lasting kindness, even if it's only sending the message that sets a time. Day five hundred twelve.

513.title: Living ashtpadi 19
513.howItsDone: Sikh teaching honors the householder's life, grihasti, and Guru Nanak's picture of the lotus untouched by the water is used for living in the world without being owned by it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karmee, and your line: kindness travels. Did you take the first step of a lasting kindness? Today we take the whole nineteenth ashtpadi off the page and into the house. Day five hundred thirteen.

Every home has one. The drawer. Dead batteries, a takeout menu from a restaurant that closed, three keys to locks nobody remembers, a charger for a phone long gone. Nobody decided to keep any of it. It just collected, the way things do when nobody's looking. And every time you open that drawer looking for scissors, you have to dig. The nineteenth ashtpadi has spent three days on what stays behind and what goes along. Living it starts somewhere very small. Maybe with that drawer.
screen: `THE DRAWER EVERY HOME HAS.` → `IT JUST COLLECTED.` → `LIVING IT STARTS SMALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the nineteenth ashtpadi in one breath: the riches, youth and power we pile up stay behind; the Name we earn and the good we do go along. So how do people actually live that? Not, in Sikh teaching, by leaving home. Guru Nanak spent his last years farming at Kartarpur, raising a family, running a community kitchen. Sikhs call that life grihasti, the householder's path, and they hold it up as a full spiritual life. So living light doesn't mean owning nothing. It means owning lightly: holding things with an open hand. Guru Nanak gave a picture for it in the Sidh Gosht, his conversation with the Siddhas, the yogi masters. In paraphrase: as the lotus floats on the water and stays untouched by it, as the duck swims the stream and stays dry. Kamal, the lotus: it lives in the pond and isn't soaked by it. In the world, not drowned in it. And then there's the drawer. It may seem silly to link a junk drawer to a hymn, but Sukhmani works on the mind, and the mind is often cluttered in exactly that way: old grudges, worries about things that never happened, plans for a version of life you outgrew. Clearing a drawer won't clear all that. But it's practice. You learn to look at something, admit you're not using it, and let it go to someone who will. That's living light: not empty hands, open ones.
screen: `STAYS BEHIND, GOES ALONG.` · `NOT RUNNING AWAY: THE HOUSEHOLDER.` · `THE LOTUS: IN THE WATER, NOT SOAKED.` · `THE DRAWER: PRACTICE LETTING GO.` · then, large: `OPEN HANDS, NOT EMPTY ONES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear out one drawer. If you can, go to it now. If you can't, picture it clearly. Take out one thing at a time and hold it for a breath. Ask: do I use this? Could someone else? Make three small piles: keep, give, throw away. Don't hurry, and don't judge yourself for what's in there. Just notice how the hand opens a little more each time. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as each thing goes. The bell holds the time.
Kamal, the lotus: the householder's way is owning lightly, like the kamal on the water, untouched by it, and letting go of what you don't use so it can move on.
Your line: live light. Today, take the give pile somewhere it will be used: a donation box, a neighbor, a friend who needs a charger. Day five hundred thirteen.

514.title: Ashtpadi 20, salok: wandering, I came
514.hook: phirat phirat: wandering and wandering, I have come to Your refuge (Sukhmani 20)
514.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twentieth ashtpadi begin with its salok, in which the seeker, after long wandering, comes to God's refuge and asks only to be joined to devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kamal, and your line: live light. Did the give pile from the drawer find a new home? Today a new ashtpadi begins, the twentieth, with a traveler who finally stops. Day five hundred fourteen.

Phirat phirat. Say it out loud and it sounds like footsteps: phirat, phirat, phirat. It's the first word of the twentieth ashtpadi, and it means wandering, turning, going round and round. A car circles a city at night, looking for an address. Left, then left again, back past the same gas station, the phone saying recalculating. And then, finally, the right door, the porch light on, and someone saying come in. Today's salok is that moment of arrival.
screen: `PHIRAT, PHIRAT: LIKE FOOTSTEPS.` → `RECALCULATING.` → `THE PORCH LIGHT ON.`

segments.voice: The salok has two lines. In paraphrase: wandering and wandering, O God, I have come, and fallen at Your sanctuary. This is Nanak's prayer, O God: attach me to Your devotion. Start with the repeated word. Gurbani often doubles a word to make it last: phirat phirat isn't one detour, it's a whole life of them. Some readers hear in it the long round of births and deaths, the soul turning through lifetime after lifetime. Others hear the ordinary wandering of a single life: job to job, want to want, one more thing that was supposed to finally make it feel settled. The text holds both. Then the verb: I have come, aaiaa. Not I have earned my way in, or I have found the answer. Just: I'm here. And then pariaa: I've fallen, or I've laid myself down, at Your saran, Your refuge. It's the posture of someone too tired to keep standing. The last line is the request. Notice what it doesn't ask for. It doesn't ask for the wandering to have been worth it, or for a prize at the end. It asks: attach me to Your bhagti, Your devotion. Keep me here. After nineteen ashtpadis of teaching, of lists and pictures and warnings, the twentieth opens with no argument at all. Just a traveler at the door, and a request to stay.
screen: `THE SALOK: I HAVE COME, I HAVE FALLEN.` · `PHIRAT PHIRAT: A WHOLE LIFE OF DETOURS.` · `NOT EARNED, JUST ARRIVED.` · `THE REQUEST: KEEP ME HERE.` · then, large: `I HAVE COME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop and rest. Wherever you are, let yourself arrive. Feel the weight of your body settle into the chair or the floor, as if you'd just walked a long way. Let the shoulders drop. With each breath out, you can silently say: I have come. Nothing to fix for two minutes, nowhere else to get to. If thoughts start wandering, notice the footsteps, phirat phirat, and come back. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Phirat, wandering, going round and round: its salok, phirat phirat, the seeker arrives after long wandering at God's refuge and asks only to be kept in devotion.
Your line: I have come. Today, the next time you walk through a door, your own or anyone's, pause on the threshold for one breath and arrive. Day five hundred fourteen.

515.title: A beggar at the door
515.hook: the soul stands like a beggar at the Lord's door (Sukhmani 20)
515.carry: the dust of good people's feet
515.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting the twentieth ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib take the posture of the jaachak, the beggar, asking God for the Name and for the dust of the feet of the holy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, phirat, and your line: I have come. Did you pause on a threshold and arrive? The traveler has reached the door. Today we find out what they say once they're standing there. Day five hundred fifteen.

Some people will carry a couch up four flights alone rather than text a friend. Some will sit up until midnight with a form they don't understand rather than ask the coworker who does. Asking is hard. It means admitting you can't do it yourself, and it means someone might say no. So it's striking that the first stanza of the twentieth ashtpadi doesn't open with a king, or a scholar, or a saint. It opens with a jaachak: a beggar, standing at the door, asking.
screen: `A COUCH, FOUR FLIGHTS, ALONE.` → `ASKING IS HARD.` → `JAACHAK: THE ONE WHO ASKS.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: the humble beggar begs God for a gift. In Your mercy, give me Your Name. Then it adds a second request: I ask for the dust of the feet of the holy. Jaachak is a beggar, one who asks for alms. Jaachai is the verb, to beg. Guru Arjan sets them side by side, the beggar begging, so you can't miss the posture. It's an old picture in Indian devotion, and Gurbani returns to it often: the soul at God's door with an empty bowl. Here's what's surprising. The beggar isn't ashamed. In Sikh thought the real trouble is haumai, the inflated self that insists it needs no one. A beggar has already let that go. They know the bowl is empty; they're not pretending otherwise. That honesty is the opening. And look at what the beggar asks for. Not money, not success, not a long life. The Name, and the dust of good people's feet. That second request sounds odd to modern ears. It's an image of deep humility: to be so low before good people that you'd count the dust they walk in as a gift. Sikhs echo it when they bow, touch the floor, or serve shoes at the gurdwara door. Yesterday we stood at God's door as a tired traveler. Today the traveler finds the words, and they turn out to be a beggar's words: the Name, and the dust of good people's feet.
screen: `JAACHAK JAACHAI: THE BEGGAR BEGS.` · `NO SHAME: THE BOWL IS EMPTY.` · `THE ASK: THE NAME, AND THE DUST.` · `THE TRAVELER FINDS THE WORDS.` · then, large: `A BEGGAR AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask humbly for one thing. Sit with your hands open, palms up, resting on your knees, like a bowl. Breathe slowly. Let one real need come to mind, something you've been trying to handle alone. Don't dress it up. Just let it be what it is. If you pray, you can hold it in your open hands and ask, the way the beggar asks. If you don't, simply notice who you could ask: a friend, a colleague, a neighbor. The bell holds the time.
Jaachak, a beggar, one who asks for alms: in Sukhmani's twentieth ashtpadi the jaachak asks God for the Name and for the dust of good people's feet.
Your line: the dust of good people's feet. Today, ask one person for help with something you'd normally carry alone. Let it be small. Day five hundred fifteen.

516.title: Mercy asked for
516.hook: the prayer asks for mercy, not reward (Sukhmani 20)
516.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twentieth ashtpadi ask for the Name with the words kar kirpaa, in Your mercy, and Gurbani links grace received with forgiveness given.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jaachak, and your line: the dust of good people's feet. Did you ask someone for help with something small? The beggar asked for the Name. Today we look at the two words that came before the asking. Day five hundred sixteen.

A loyalty card at a coffee shop. Ten stamps, and the eleventh cup is free. It's a tidy little deal: you do this, you get that. A lot of life runs like that card, and a lot of religion is imagined that way too. Pray enough, give enough, behave well enough, and eventually the reward is stamped and due. Sukhmani's twentieth ashtpadi tucks two small words into the beggar's request that tear the card in half. Kar kirpaa. Today: mercy, asked for.
screen: `TEN STAMPS, ONE FREE CUP.` → `DO THIS, GET THAT.` → `KAR KIRPAA.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's stanza, in paraphrase: the beggar begs for a gift; in Your mercy, give me Your Name. Kar kirpaa: do mercy, show kindness. Kirpaa is grace or mercy, a gift given because the giver is kind, not because the receiver has filled a card. And the word for what's asked, daan, is a gift too: alms, charity. Nothing in that sentence is owed. Day five hundred met the same thread in Japji: actions shape a life, but grace, nadar, opens the gate. Today it's in the beggar's own mouth. Deeds matter; Sikhs are expected to work, serve, and live well. But what the beggar asks for isn't bought by them. It's given, the way a gift is given. Why does that matter on an ordinary Tuesday? Because how you think you're treated tends to become how you treat others. If everything is earned, then the people who've hurt you owe you, and the debt can feel permanent. If you've been met with mercy, the ledger loosens. There's a salok of the poet-saint Kabir, recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib, that makes the link plainly. In paraphrase: where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself. Khimaa, forgiveness, is mercy turned outward. The beggar who asks for kirpaa learns, slowly, to give some away.
screen: `KAR KIRPAA: IN YOUR MERCY.` · `DAAN: A GIFT, NOT WAGES.` · `ASKED AS A GIFT, NOT BOUGHT.` · `KHIMAA: MERCY TURNED OUTWARD.` · then, large: `MERCY, NOT REWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive someone. Start small. Not the deepest wound; one of the little ones. A friend who canceled, a driver who cut you off, a sibling's careless comment. Sit, breathe slowly, and picture them. Notice the ledger in your chest: they owe me. On each breath out, loosen it a little. You don't have to excuse what happened. You're simply choosing not to keep stamping the card. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you let go. The bell holds the time.
Kirpaa, mercy or grace: the beggar asks with kar kirpaa, in Your kirpaa, and the Name is given as a gift, not earned as a wage.
Your line: mercy, not reward. Today, when someone falls short, try answering with a little more mercy than they've earned. Day five hundred sixteen.

517.title: Living ashtpadi 20
517.hook: refuge is a place you can return to
517.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 21, salok: when there was nothing
517.howItsDone: Sikh practice returns to God's refuge daily, sitting with the Name at amrit vela before dawn and reciting Sohila at night, and gurdwaras keep their doors and kitchens open to all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirpaa, and your line: mercy, not reward. Did you give someone a little more mercy than they'd earned? Today we carry the whole twentieth ashtpadi out of the book. Day five hundred seventeen.

There's an old man in a lot of neighborhoods who has a bench. Same bench, same park, every morning, coffee in a paper cup. Nobody owns a park bench, but everyone knows it's his. And if you asked him why he comes, he probably wouldn't say anything grand. He'd say: it's where I sit. A refuge doesn't have to be a fortress. Sometimes it's just a place you keep coming back to, until coming back is part of who you are. That's how the twentieth ashtpadi gets lived.
screen: `THE SAME BENCH EVERY MORNING.` → `IT'S WHERE I SIT.` → `A PLACE YOU COME BACK TO.`

segments.voice: Here's the twentieth ashtpadi in brief. A traveler, after long wandering, phirat phirat, comes to God's saran, God's refuge, and falls there. Standing at the door, the traveler becomes a beggar, asking for the Name and the dust of good people's feet, and asking it as mercy, not reward. Saran is the key word. It means shelter, sanctuary, protection. In Sukhmani it's God's saran, a refuge that's God's to give. And in Sikh practice it isn't somewhere you reach once and never leave. The traveler came after wandering, and minds wander again. So refuge is something you return to. Daily. That's partly what the daily banis are for. Sikh practice sets aside the early hours, amrit vela, the ambrosial time before dawn, for sitting with the Name, and closes the day with Sohila. The days between can be loud; the refuge is there at both ends. Gurdwaras carry the same idea in stone. The Darbar Sahib in Amritsar has doors on all four sides, which Sikhs explain as open to anyone, from any direction. Gurdwaras keep a langar for whoever comes, and travelers find a meal there, and often a place to rest. And it doesn't have to be a building. For one person it's a corner of a bedroom with a small shelf. For another, a walk at dawn. The place matters less than the returning.
screen: `THE ASHTPADI: ARRIVE, ASK, RECEIVE.` · `SARAN: SHELTER THAT IS GOD'S TO GIVE.` · `RETURNED TO DAILY, AT BOTH ENDS.` · `DOORS ON FOUR SIDES.` · then, large: `REFUGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your quiet place. Look around the space you're in, or picture your home. Where could you sit for two minutes and not be interrupted? A chair by a window, the edge of a bed, a step outside. Go there now if you can, or picture it closely. Settle in. Breathe slowly. Let this become the spot you come back to. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru here. The bell holds the time.
Saran, refuge or sanctuary: God's saran isn't reached once and left; Sikh practice returns to it daily, morning and night.
Your line: refuge. Today, come back to your quiet place one more time before you sleep, even for three breaths. Day five hundred seventeen.

518.title: Ashtpadi 21, salok: when there was nothing
518.hook: sargun nirgun nirankaar: the Formless, with and without qualities, rested in the void (Sukhmani 21)
518.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-first ashtpadi begin with a salok picturing God, with and without qualities, resting in sunn, the stillness before creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saran, and your line: refuge. Did you go back to your quiet place? A week ends today. It began with karmee, kindness travels, then live light; then a wanderer arrived, begged at the door, and asked for mercy. Now Sukhmani goes back before everything. Day five hundred eighteen.

Before a concert begins, there's a moment. The lights dim, the coughing stops, the conductor lifts the baton, and for two or three seconds a whole hall full of people holds absolutely still. It's not empty, exactly. It's full of everything that's about to happen. Some musicians say the piece really starts there, in that silence. The twenty-first ashtpadi of Sukhmani goes looking for the silence before the biggest piece of all: the moment before there was anything. Its word is sunn.
screen: `THE HALL HOLDS ITS BREATH.` → `NOT EMPTY: FULL OF WHAT'S COMING.` → `SUNN.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: with qualities and without them, the Formless One was Himself absorbed in the stillness of the void. He made it all Himself, Nanak, and He Himself remembers it again. Three words to open, and day five hundred one already met them. Sargun: with qualities, the One you can describe, near and present in the world. Nirgun: without qualities, beyond every description. Nirankaar: the Formless. The salok says all three in one breath, and none of them cancels the others. Then sunn, which is today's word. It comes from the Sanskrit shunya, empty. But in Gurbani sunn isn't a bleak nothing. It's the deep stillness God rested in before any world existed, sunn samaadhi, absorbed in the void, the way the hall is absorbed in silence before the music. Guru Nanak describes the same scene elsewhere, in the raag Maru: for countless ages there was only darkness, no earth, no sky, only the infinite will. Gurbani doesn't try to give a date or a mechanism. It doesn't say how long, or what the stillness was like from inside. The sources are silent there, and Sukhmani is content to leave it that way. What it gives instead is a starting point for wonder: in Sukhmani's telling, before anything there was the One, at rest, and everything came out of that stillness.
screen: `SARGUN, NIRGUN, NIRANKAAR: ONE BREATH.` · `SUNN: FROM SHUNYA, EMPTY.` · `NOT A BLEAK NOTHING: GOD'S STILLNESS.` · `NO DATE, NO MECHANISM: JUST WONDER.` · then, large: `WHEN THERE WAS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in silence. Turn off what can be turned off. Close your eyes or let them rest on the floor. You don't need to empty your mind; just stop adding to it. Listen to the quiet underneath the small sounds: the fridge, the traffic, your own breath. Let it be like the hall before the music. Full, and still. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru without saying anything at all. The bell holds the time.
Sunn. The stillness, or void, in which the Formless One rested before creation; from the root of the word for empty, but in Gurbani full of God.
Your line: when there was nothing. Today, find one silence, a pause in a conversation or before you start the car, and let it be full instead of awkward. Day five hundred eighteen.

myth: in Gurbani, sunn means a bleak, empty nothing
it's the deep stillness God rested in before creation.
the salok pictures God resting in sunn before creation
sunn samaadhi: absorbed in the stillness, like a hall before the music.
Gurbani gives a date for when creation began
it gives no date or mechanism; the sources are silent there.

fork.setup: the hall goes still before the music. by the salok, what was the stillness before creation?
options: empty: nothing at all.
a pause between two old worlds.
full: the One, absorbed in stillness.
fork.reveal: sunn samaadhi: in Gurbani the stillness is God's own, not a bleak nothing, and the salok adds that He made it all Himself.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sunn, the stillness or void before creation; from Sanskrit shunya, empty.

trapdoor: what you thought: sunn means nothing at all.
what it means: the full, deep stillness in which the Formless One rested before anything was made.
what a scholar hears: sunn comes from Sanskrit shunya, the root behind the Indian word for zero, but Gurbani's sunn samaadhi is God's absorbed stillness, not mere absence.
